summary: Defines a C-language application programming interface for the Lightweight Directory Access Protocol, so that programs can search and modify directories. It is informational.

eli5.summary: A set of ready-made tools a programmer can call to ask a directory questions without learning the details.

how to call ldap from c
how to open an ldap connection in c
subtitle: A C library interface that lets programs open, search and change a directory over LDAP.

tldr.problem: Programs that want to look up or change directory information over LDAP need a simple, common way to call the protocol from C.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC defines a set of C calls: open a connection, bind (authenticate), search or modify, parse the results, and unbind. Every operation comes in a synchronous form and an asynchronous form.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational memo, not a standard. It gives programmers one vocabulary of calls such as ldap_open(), ldap_search_s() and ldap_unbind().

facts.label: Transport
facts.value: TCP connection to an LDAP server

today: RFC 1823 is an Informational memo from August 1995, and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It describes the C API as of that date.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
RFC 1823 defines a C language application program interface to the lightweight directory access protocol (LDAP). The authors say it is designed to be powerful, yet simple to use.

It offers compatible synchronous and asynchronous interfaces, so that it suits a wide variety of applications. The document gives a short overview of the LDAP model, then of how a program uses the API, then each call in detail, and ends with sample code in an appendix.
sections.eli5: This is an instruction book for programmers who want their C program to look things up in a big electronic address book. It lists the buttons they can press.

sections.title: The LDAP Model
sections.content:
LDAP is based on a client-server model: a client makes a TCP connection to an LDAP server, then sends requests and receives responses. It can be a lightweight front end to the X.500 directory, or a stand-alone service.

Information is stored in entries, each describing some object such as a person. An entry is made of attributes, and each attribute has a type and one or more values. An attribute's syntax decides what values are allowed (for example ASCII text or a jpeg photograph) and how they behave, such as whether case matters when comparing.

Entries form a tree. Each entry is named among its siblings by a relative distinguished name (RDN), and the full distinguished name (DN) joins the RDNs from the root down. The RFC's example is cn=Barbara Jensen, o=University of Michigan, c=US.
sections.eli5: Think of a family tree of cards. Each card describes one thing, like a person, and has labelled lines on it. A card's full name is the path from the top of the tree down to that card.

sections.title: Opening, Binding and Closing
sections.content:
An application uses the API in four steps: open a connection, authenticate, perform operations, and close the connection.

ldap_open() takes a space-separated list of hostnames and a TCP port number, tries the hosts in order, and returns a connection handle (or NULL on failure). The constant LDAP_PORT gives the default port. One of the bind calls must complete before any other operation is attempted on the connection.

The bind calls come in three kinds: ldap_simple_bind() with a password, ldap_kerberos_bind(), and the general ldap_bind() with a method of LDAP_AUTH_SIMPLE, LDAP_AUTH_KRBV41 or LDAP_AUTH_KRBV42. Later bind calls can re-authenticate on the same connection. ldap_unbind() works synchronously, closes the connection and frees the handle, which is invalid afterwards.
sections.eli5: You first dial the directory's number, then show your ID, then ask your questions, and finally hang up. You must show your ID before the directory will answer anything.

sections.title: Searching and Changing Entries
sections.content:
Searching uses ldap_search() and its synchronous forms ldap_search_s() and ldap_search_st() (which adds a timeout). A search takes a base DN, a scope (LDAP_SCOPE_BASE, LDAP_SCOPE_ONELEVEL or LDAP_SCOPE_SUBTREE), a filter string as described in RFC 1558, and the list of attributes to return. Passing NULL for the list returns all available attributes.

Three fields of the connection handle shape a search: ld_sizelimit and ld_timelimit (zero means no limit) and ld_deref, which says how aliases are handled.

LDAP has no direct read or list operation. Reading an entry is emulated by a search with base scope, and listing children by a one-level search, both with the filter (objectclass=*). Other calls are ldap_modify() (add, delete or replace attribute values, in the order listed), ldap_modrdn(), ldap_add() and ldap_delete(). An added entry's parent must already exist, and a deleted entry must be a leaf.
sections.eli5: You can ask the directory to find cards that match a description, change what is written on a card, rename a card, add a new card or throw one away. A card can only be thrown away if nothing hangs below it.

sections.title: Getting and Parsing Results
sections.content:
Results come back in an opaque LDAPMessage structure. A program must not look inside it, but steps through it with ldap_first_entry() and ldap_next_entry(), then through each entry's attributes with ldap_first_attribute() and ldap_next_attribute(), and reads values with ldap_get_values().

The _len variants, such as ldap_get_values_len(), return berval structures and are the form to use for binary data like images. Values and results are allocated for the caller, so they should be freed with calls such as ldap_value_free() and ldap_msgfree(). Names are handled by ldap_get_dn(), ldap_explode_dn() and ldap_dn2ufn().
sections.eli5: The answer arrives in a sealed envelope. Special helper tools open it, hand you one card at a time and read each line on the card. When you are done you must throw the envelope away.

sections.title: Synchronous Calls, Asynchronous Calls and Errors
sections.content:
Synchronous calls have names ending in _s and return an outcome such as LDAP_SUCCESS or another error code. Asynchronous calls return a message id, which is passed to ldap_result() to collect the outcome. ldap_abandon() abandons an operation in progress, and on failure asynchronous calls return -1 and set ld_errno.

For ldap_result(), a NULL timeout blocks until a result arrives and a zero timeout polls; it returns 0 if the timeout expires. Errors are interpreted with ldap_result2error(), ldap_err2string() and ldap_perror(). The RFC lists about forty named codes, such as LDAP_NO_SUCH_OBJECT, LDAP_INVALID_CREDENTIALS and LDAP_SERVER_DOWN.

The Security Considerations section is a single sentence: LDAP supports minimal security during connection authentication.
sections.eli5: You can wait at the counter for your answer, or take a ticket number and come back later to collect it. If something goes wrong, there are tools that turn the error number into a sentence you can read.
